items.title: Sikkim district judge moves Supreme Court against High Court, alleges vindictive vigilance action
items.summary: A sitting district judge in Sikkim has approached the Supreme Court against the Sikkim High Court, alleging that he has been subjected to a sustained campaign of harassment and retaliatory vigilance action after he complained against a then sitting judge of the High Court, who is now retired. District and Sessions Judge at Mangan, Prajwal Khatiwada , has filed a writ petition under Article 32 challenging a show cause notice issued to him by the High Court of Sikkim on August 12. The petition names the High Court of Sikkim, its Registrar (Vigilance), Vigilance Inspector Sarad Subba and the State of Sikkim as respondents. Khatiwada joined the Sikkim Judicial Service in 2005 after topping the State's judicial service examination. He served as Registrar General of the High Court from February 2023 to December 2025 before being posted to Mangan. According to the petition, the trouble started after Khatiwada lodged a formal complaint on December 12, 2025 against a then sitting judge of the High Court, alleging mistreatment and humiliation. Copies of the complaint were sent to the Chief Justice of India and the four senior-most judges of the Supreme Court. The High Court judge in question was appointed Acting Chief Justice of the Sikkim High Court days later, with effect from December 15, 2025, after the previous Chief Justice demitted office. The petition alleges that from that point on, Khatiwada was targeted through a series of administrative actions. These include his abrupt transfer, withdrawal of his security cover, questioning of his subordinate staff about his personal matters and the initiation of vigilance inquiries against him. items.title: Prajwal Revanna sent to police custody for two days over mobile phone use in prison
items.summary: A Bengaluru court on Tuesday sent former MP Prajwal Revanna to police custody for two days in connection with the alleged use of mobile phone inside Parappana Agrahara Central Prison where he lodged for rape case. Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate Sandeep Patil passed the order after hearing the prosecution and defence. Sandeep Patil Prajwal Revanna, who represented the Hassan parliamentary constituency from 2019 to 2023, is serving life sentence after being convicted of rape in August 2025. The present case stemmed from a raid conducted by Central Crime Branch (CCB) which allegedly led to recovery of mobile phones and other digital devices from Revanna. According to the complaint, the CCB recovered a Redmi 5G smartphone, a blue packet notebook, a charger and a SanDisk pen drive from a high-security barrack during a raid conducted on August 11. Revanna allegedly claimed that the notebook belonged to him. The police claimed that they found Facebook, WhatsApp, Instagram, Netflix, Prime Video and other applications installed on the smartphone. The device was password-protected and was subsequently sent to the Forensic Science Laboratory for examination. According to the prosecution, phone was allegedly being used to communicate with Revanna's family members and lawyers and the SIM card was procured from Andhra Pradesh. The police registered a case for fraudulent concealment of property under Section 323 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) and for offences under the Karnataka Prisons (Amendment) Act, 2022. Assistant Public Prosecutor Satish Rao submitted that prison officials and staff have also been made accused in the case and that the investigation is required to determine how a mobile phone, charger and other articles came into the possession of the accused. He argued that the accused cannot be properly interrogated in prison and hence, sought their custody for the purpose of investigation. Advocate Arun G, appearing for Revanna, opposed the plea. He submitted that the Parappana Agrahara police station is located opposite the prison and that the police could go there and conduct the investigation instead of taking Prajwal into custody. After hearing the submissions, the Court directed that Revanna and another accused Prathap Rai be sent to police custody for 2 days. The case will be heard next on September 10.

items.title: Prisoners in Punjab become drug-dependent after entering jail: P&H High Court calls situation serious
items.summary: The Punjab and Haryana High Court on Tuesday expressed serious concern over the fact that many prisoners in Punjab become drug-dependent after their entry into the jails [Court On Its Own Motion v State of Punjab and Others]. A Bench of Chief Justice Ashwani Kumar Mishra and Justice Rohit Kapoor observed that in the absence of any strategy to cure the inmates' drug dependence, they will never be able to fully avail of their right to life as the continued drug dependence would cause further crises in their lives. The official data submitted before the Court on September 1 had revealed that 44 percent (15,768 out of 35,449) of the prisoners lodged in jails across Punjab are dependent on drugs. Today, the Court noted that about 83 percent of these inmates were registered with the Out Patient Opioid Assisted Treatment Clinic (OOAT Clinic) only after their jail entry. "Learned Amicus Curiae has pointed out from the affidavit filed by the State of Punjab on the previous occasion that, at the time of entry into jail, 2540 inmates were already registered under the Out Patient Opioid Assisted Treatment Clinic (OOAT Clinic) and were being administered tablets/medicines prior to their admission. The number of inmates who presently are drug dependent is 15768," the Bench recorded in today's order. Chief Justice Ashwani Kumar Mishra and Justice Rohit Kapoor The Court observed that the data prima facie indicated the prevalence of a serious malaise in Punjab prisons. "It shows that not only are those entering jail, drug dependent, but there is a growth of almost 4-5 times in the number of jail inmates who become drug dependent after their entry into jail," the Court added. It directed the Punjab government to inform the Court regarding implementation of a prison rule requiring the State to implement a scientific de-addiction programme for drug addicts to cure them and restore them to society as useful citizens. It also asked the Union of India to place on record the methodology suggested for bringing such drug-dependent inmates to a state of normalcy. "We may indicate that this is a serious issue, and we expect the authorities to remain alive to their obligations to help such inmates in securing their right to life under the Constitution of India," the Court said. items.title: The public law overhang in arbitration: Does the public sector trigger differential judicial oversight?
items.summary: On paper, India appears arbitration-friendly. The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, based on the UNCITRAL Model Law, was enacted to make arbitration a final, efficient and autonomous method of commercial dispute resolution, subject to narrowly circumscribed judicial supervision. Over 3 decades, the Supreme Court repeatedly affirmed party autonomy, finality of awards and limited judicial intervention. Yet, a second, less predictable line of decisions has emerged. These decisions commonly involve large public infrastructure projects, substantial claims against the State or State-owned entities and judicial interventions that would be surprising in purely private commercial disputes. This article argues that the tension is institutional rather than doctrinal: constitutional courts in India, accustomed to supervising public administration and protecting the public exchequer, sometimes carry public law instincts into commercial adjudication when the State is a party. The result is not an explicit re-writing of arbitration law, but a gradual shift in how courts apply its limits. A special challenge for Indian arbitration jurisprudence is maintaining the conceptual separation between public law adjudication and private commercial adjudication where the State is a litigant. Section 34 limits grounds for setting aside an award to a few procedural and substantive defects: incapacity, invalid arbitration agreement, denial of opportunity to present one’s case, decisions beyond the scope of reference, defects in tribunal constitution, non-arbitrability and awards contrary to “public policy of India.” The 2015 Amendment narrowed public policy with two important explanations: Explanation 1 confines “public policy” to awards induced by fraud or corruption, awards contrary to the fundamental policy of Indian law, or those that offend the most basic notions of morality or justice.
